questions.stem: How does Data-As-a-Product (DAaP) differ from a traditional data product?
options: DAaP is a curated, production-grade dataset or model designed for consumption by multiple downstream users, systems or applications, rather than a narrow, predefined use case
DAaP is always a dashboard, whereas traditional data products are always datasets
DAaP is stored only in memory for speed
DAaP is built exclusively by external vendors
DAaP has no owner, whereas traditional data products do
questions.explanation: Traditional data products serve narrow, predefined use cases; DAaP is curated and production-grade, designed for consumption by many downstream users, systems or applications.

questions.stem: Which two pathways lead a data product to become Data-As-a-Product (DAaP)?
options: Migration and replication
Organic maturity and purposeful design
Certification and audit
Outsourcing and insourcing
Archiving and restoration
questions.explanation: A data product evolves into DAaP either through organic maturity, when its utility extends beyond its original intent, or through purposeful design from day one.

questions.stem: A regional sales insights dashboard's curated datasets start feeding forecasting models, executive dashboards and marketing analytics. Which DAaP pathway does this illustrate?
options: Purposeful design
Decommissioning
Organic maturity
Cost allocation
Dependency shifting
questions.explanation: This is the organic maturity example: the dashboard's utility extended beyond its original intent and began powering other systems.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed as a core feature that a data product must demonstrate to qualify as DAaP?
options: Semantic modelling and clarity
Enforced data contracts
Discoverability and accessibility
Exclusive single-consumer access
Independent lifecycle management
questions.explanation: DAaP is designed for multiple consumers; exclusive single-consumer access contradicts its purpose, whereas the other four are listed core features.

questions.stem: What must enforced data contracts in DAaP codify and version?
options: Employee names and departments
Only the price charged to consumers
The colour scheme of dashboards
The hardware specification of servers
Schemas, data types, expected freshness and delivery protocols
questions.explanation: Enforced data contracts codify and version schemas, data types, expected freshness and delivery protocols to ensure consumer confidence and system interoperability.

questions.stem: What is a dependency web in the context of DAaP?
options: The situation where a DAaP serves many consumers, so modifying or decommissioning its originating system risks cascading failures
A website listing all data products
A network diagram of servers in a data centre
The set of people who report to the Data Product Owner
A graph of customer relationships
questions.explanation: Because a DAaP serves a variety of consumers, changes to or decommissioning of the originating system can break those dependencies and cause cascading failures.

questions.stem: When a DAaP faces decommissioning, what is the stated downside of shifting dependencies so that consumers source data directly from origin systems?
options: It makes the DAaP more expensive to run
It increases integration effort and consumer-side complexity
It removes all governance from the data
It requires a new database technology
It forces producers to retain the DAaP indefinitely
questions.explanation: Shifting dependencies reduces DAaP operational overhead but increases integration effort and consumer-side complexity.

questions.stem: Why do ownership and funding conflicts arise as a DAaP grows in reach?
options: Because regulators require a single funder for every dataset
Because DAaP cannot be shared across more than two teams
Because producers may resist carrying the operational burden while consumers are reluctant to own upstream complexity
Because the cost of storage always doubles each year
Because data contracts forbid cost sharing
questions.explanation: As reach grows, ambiguity surfaces around maintenance responsibilities and funding: producers resist the operational burden and consumers avoid upstream complexity.

questions.stem: Which DAaP management strategy recommends architecting DAaPs as composable services so they can be selectively migrated or deprecated?
options: Monitor usage patterns
Implement cost allocation models
Embed collaborative governance
Design for modularity
Plan decommissioning at inception
questions.explanation: Designing for modularity means building DAaPs as composable services, allowing selective migration or deprecation without ecosystem-wide disruption.

questions.stem: What does 'Plan decommissioning at inception' mean for a DAaP?
options: Every DAaP should be shut down within its first year
A DAaP should never be decommissioned once built
Decommissioning should be decided only by the consumers
A DAaP should be built without any consumers
Every DAaP should have a sunset strategy aligned with downstream transition plans from the start
questions.explanation: Planning decommissioning at inception means every DAaP has a sunset strategy aligned with downstream transition plans, minimising reactive disruption.
